newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan peace talks with gangs advance.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan peace talks with gangs advance.

text.p: Dozens of members of an armed gang left over from Nicaragua's civil war have laid down their arms amid advances in peace talks between armed gangs and the government, top government officials said on Monday.

President Arnoldo Aleman told a news conference 27 members of an armed gang led by Commander Porfirio Bravo Lacayo disarmed on Saturday in El Coral, Chontales, 135 miles (215 kms) southeast of the capital Managua, in exchange for amnesty and land.

The demobilization brought the total number of gang members who have disarmed since peace talks began early in February to about 50. These gangs are loosely linked to former Contra rebels or the Sandinista army,
Before the talks started, the army estimated 500 gang members operated in parts of north and central Nicaragua.
"Today, it gives us pleasure to announce that no armed gangs exist in the department of Chontales since all of them laid down their arms on Saturday night," Aleman said.

On Feb. 14, 23 members of two armed gangs in Nicaragua's South Atlantic Autonomous Region laid down their arms in what was the first success of the government's campaign to have all the armed gangs demobilized by Feb. 28.

Aleman said government officials were making "the final arrangements" with the remaining armed gangs, mainly in the northern province of Jinotega, and he expected to make the Feb. 28 demobilization deadline.

In exchange for disarming, each gang member would get 10 to 17 acres (four to seven hectares) of land, material to build a house, agricultural training and an amnesty from prosecution, Interior Minister Jose Antonio Alvarado said.
Once the peace talks have concluded, all remaining armed gangs that have not accepted the terms of the government's amnesty would be treated as common criminals, Aleman said.
Nicaragua's civil war ended in 1990 but many former combatants later re-armed to protest what they said was the government's failure to fulfil the terms of the peace treaty.

The armed gangs have not gone away despite repeated government amnesties and help reintegrating into civilian life. Since 1990, armed bands have killed 1,000 people, wounded 400 and kidnapped 600 civilians, the army says.
